Limits and theory

Source: vignettes/limits-theory.Rmd
limits-theory.Rmd

Every answer of variplex rests on the graphs, and the graphs hold relationships between two features. This vignette shows what that means: first on one example, with every function at once; then measured, as the share of the configurations allowed by the graphs that are valid (their representativeness); then function by function. The second half explains where the limits come from: rules that tie three or more features, and, for UVL models, numbers and texts that a logic formula cannot hold. It ends with the proofs that what the graphs say is true, and that about one or two features they say everything.

band <- vp_generate(
  vp_example("miband3_realized.uvl"),
  or_graph = TRUE,
  representativeness = TRUE
)
battery <- vp_generate(
  vp_example("miband3_battery.uvl"),
  or_graph = TRUE,
  representativeness = TRUE
)
# the 24 valid bands, one per row
products <- read.csv(vp_example("miband3_products.csv"))

representativeness = TRUE needs the model counter GANAK (see Measuring your own model).

One rule, three features, and every function

Add to the Mi Band 3 a battery rule: the battery cannot power NFC, the heart-rate sensor and the touch screen at once. The example miband3_battery.uvl is the band with this one more line:

!(NFC & HeartRateSensor & TouchScreen)

Every pair of the three is still possible, so no relationship between two features changes. Ask the functions of the package:

vp_compare(band, battery) |> select(graph, gained, lost, jaccard)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 4
#>   graph      gained  lost jaccard
#>   <chr>       <int> <int>   <dbl>
#> 1 requires        0     0       1
#> 2 excludes        0     0       1
#> 3 atleastone      0     0       1
identical(vp_feature_table(band), vp_feature_table(battery))
#> [1] TRUE
identical(
  vp_summary(band) |> select(-model),
  vp_summary(battery) |> select(-model)
)
#> [1] FALSE

For every function the two models are the same. Yet the battery rule removed 4 of the 24 products:

nrow(products)
#> [1] 24
nrow(read.csv(vp_example("miband3_battery_products.csv")))
#> [1] 20
vp_can_go_together(battery, c("TouchScreen", "HeartRateSensor", "NFC"))
#> # A tibble: 1 x 3
#>   wish                              possible reasons
#>   <chr>                             <lgl>    <chr>  
#> 1 TouchScreen, HeartRateSensor, NFC TRUE     ""

The last answer is wrong: no band of the new model has the three features, and vp_can_go_together() says TRUE. It is the one kind of mistake the functions make: they never call impossible what is possible, but they can call possible what a rule over three or more features forbids. How representative are the graphs? measures how often that happens in real models; for wish lists of a few features, rarely.

How much the graphs leave out: representativeness

The share of the configurations the graphs allow that are valid

Function: vp_representativeness()

The question. The graphs never forbid a valid configuration, but they allow some configurations that are not valid. How many?

Decide, for every feature that can vary, whether it is selected: that is a configuration of those features. The graphs allow the configuration when it breaks none of their links: no arrow goes from a selected feature to one left out, no conflict joins two selected features, and no at-least-one line joins two features left out. Every valid configuration is allowed, because every link holds in every valid configuration. But some allowed configurations are not valid: they break a rule over three or more features. The representativeness of the graphs is the share of the configurations they allow that are valid: representativeness=valid configurations of the modelconfigurations allowed by the graphs.\text{representativeness} = \frac{\text{valid configurations of the model}}{\text{configurations allowed by the graphs}} . It is 1 (100 %) when the graphs say everything the model says about its features; the rest is what they leave out.

How it is measured. Counting either number by trying every configuration is only possible for tiny models (vp_count_graph_products(), below, does it up to 20 features). For real models variplex uses a model counter, GANAK, which counts the solutions of a formula without listing them: run vp_generate() with representativeness = TRUE, as at the top of this vignette (GANAK must be installed; the argument ganak gives its path).

It counts two formulas, which it keeps in the folder of the run: __count_formula.cnf, the model, counted on the features of the graphs only, and __count_graphs.cnf, the graphs written as a formula (one clause per link). The two numbers and their ratio go into __summary.json, and the model holds them:

vp_representativeness(band)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 5
#>   vm_configurations graph_configurations share left_out note 
#>               <dbl>                <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl> <chr>
#> 1                24                   42 0.571    0.429 ""
vp_representativeness(battery)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 5
#>   vm_configurations graph_configurations share left_out note 
#>               <dbl>                <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl> <chr>
#> 1                20                   42 0.476    0.524 ""
vp_count_graph_products(band) |> select(and_atleastone)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 1
#>   and_atleastone
#>            <int>
#> 1             42

vm_configurations is the number of valid configurations of the variability model, graph_configurations the number of configurations that the graphs allow, share their ratio and left_out the rest. The graphs of the Mi Band 3 allow 42 configurations, and 24 of them are valid bands: a representativeness of 57.1 %. The 18 that are not valid break rules over three features, such as “a band with BLE has version 4.0 or 4.2”. For a model this small, vp_count_graph_products() finds the same 42 by trying every configuration: the two counts agree.

The one number that sees the battery rule. In One rule, three features, and every function, every function of the vignettes gave the same answer for the band with and without the battery rule, because no relationship between two features changed. Representativeness does change: the graphs still allow 42 configurations, but the model now has 20 valid ones, so the share falls to 47.6 %. It is the way to measure, for a model of any size, how much its graphs leave out. vp_summary() reports it in the column representativeness.

Whole configurations and wish lists. Representativeness is about whole configurations, where every feature is decided. A wish list decides only some features, and the graphs judge wish lists far better than whole configurations. Take the configuration of the band with a screen (and the OLED panel and the capacity button that come with it) and none of the other features. The graphs allow it: it breaks no link. It is not valid: a band with a screen has BLE, and a band with BLE needs version 4.0 or 4.2, a rule over three features, and this configuration has neither. Now take the wish list “a screen”. It does not say anything about the versions, so the missing version can be added, and the wish list can be built: the graphs, which say yes, are right. A rule over three features of the kind “one of these” can always be satisfied by the features a wish list leaves open; it only bites when every feature is decided. That is why, for the band, the graphs say yes to 519 wish lists and all of them can be built (100 %), while only 57.1 % of the whole configurations they allow are valid:

features <- vp_features(band) |> filter(status == "variable") |> pull(feature)
# all the 2047 wish lists of the band: every set of 1 to 11 features
wishes_all <- unlist(
  lapply(1:11, function(k) combn(features, k, simplify = FALSE)),
  recursive = FALSE
)
graph_yes <- vp_can_go_together(band, wishes_all)$possible
buildable <- vapply(
  wishes_all, # some valid band has them all
  function(w) any(rowSums(products[w]) == length(w)),
  TRUE
)
c(
  graphs_say_yes = sum(graph_yes),
  and_can_be_built = sum(graph_yes & buildable)
)
#>   graphs_say_yes and_can_be_built 
#>              519              519

Rules of the other kind, “not all of these”, do bite wish lists: with the battery rule, the wish list “NFC, heart-rate sensor and touch screen” is allowed by the graphs and cannot be built (One rule, three features, and every function). In real models measures wish lists on real models.

Why it matters. Representativeness tells how far every other answer of the vignettes can be trusted for whole products: a model whose graphs are 100 % representative is fully described by its pairs, and every question about it can be answered from the graphs alone; a model at 10 % needs a solver for every question about complete products.

Limits: what this cannot tell you

  • It is about whole configurations. As shown above, a low representativeness does not mean that the answers of vp_can_go_together() about wish lists are often wrong: the rules of the kind “one of these” lower representativeness but not the answers for wish lists.

  • It counts the Boolean formula: for a UVL model, the numbers, texts and cardinalities that the formula leaves out are left out of the count too (Features that are more than yes or no).

  • Counting is hard in general: GANAK is fast for most models, and can take long for the largest ones. If it cannot run, vp_generate() writes the graphs anyway, records the reason, and vp_representativeness() returns NA with that reason in note.

  • The counts can be huge (Linux has more configurations than atoms in the universe); R keeps about 15 digits of them, and the exact values are in __summary.json.

  • It is measured on the whole model: vp_subset() does not carry it over to a part.

Counting by trying every configuration, on a small model

Function: vp_count_graph_products()

The question. Can representativeness be checked without GANAK?

For a small model, yes: try every selection of the features that can vary and count those that break no link, graph by graph:

vp_count_graph_products(band)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 4
#>   selections respect_requires and_excludes and_atleastone
#>        <dbl>            <int>        <int>          <int>
#> 1       2048              120           48             42
nrow(products)
#> [1] 24
vp_count_graph_products(band, products = 24) |> select(bits_model, explained)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>   bits_model explained
#>        <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1       6.42     0.874

Of the 2112^{11} selections, 120 respect the requires graph, 48 also the excludes graph, and 42 all three graphs. The model itself has 24 valid products (the file miband3_products.csv of the examples, found by trying every combination of the formula). The difference, 18 selections, is what the rules over three features forbid: a band with a screen and no version of BLE, for instance. Given the number of products, the function also says how much of the model the graphs explain, on a scale of yes/no choices: the model takes away 6.4 of the 11 choices, and the graphs alone 87 % of that.

Why it matters. It makes representativeness concrete on small models and teaching examples, where every number can be checked by hand, and shows how much each graph contributes to describing the products.

Limits: what this cannot tell you

Only for small models: it tries 2n2^n selections, and refuses above 20 features. On a real model, use vp_representativeness() (above).

The limits, operation by operation

The table repeats, in two questions, the boxes Limits of the vignettes. Is what the operation says true? And does it say everything?

Operation Is what it says true? Does it say everything?
Reading (vp_read, vp_read_history) Yes. The files of variplex, as they are. No. Relationships between two features only; for UVL, no numbers or texts; features matched across versions by name.
Reading old graphs with artificial = "drop" No. Not always: a rule on names can drop a real option or keep a helper. No. As above.
Minimal form, expansion (vp_minimal, vp_expand) Yes. The same information as the complete graphs. No. As the complete graphs; and “what was written” only roughly.
Part of a model (vp_subset) Yes. Exact (property P3, Three properties of the graphs). No. As the graphs.
Tree of a UVL file (vp_read_uvl_tree) Yes. The tree as written. No. Attributes, cardinalities and imports are not read.
Drawing (vp_plot) Yes. Every link drawn is in what was given. No. Positions are the choice of the layout, not a measure.
Measures of a feature (vp_feature_table) Yes. Exact counts on the graphs. No. A rule over three features adds nothing to them.
Lists of a feature (vp_required_by, …) Yes. Yes for relationships between two features; no for rules over three.
Genuine hubs, warning zone Yes, for the threshold chosen. No. They depend on the threshold, and on the requires graph.
Atomic sets Yes. Yes. Every group of features always selected together.
Skeleton, levels, depth, width, chains Yes. Exact on the requires graph. No. The skeleton is not the list of constraints; rules over three features count only through the arrows they imply.
Longest chain of decisions Yes. Each step forces the next. No. Decisions forced only by two decisions together are not seen.
Largest free set (vp_largest_free_set) Yes, every two of its features are free; the largest one up to 60 features, a large one above. No. Free in pairs is not free together (Width and chains).
Foundations, leaves Yes. No. A rule over three features can still lean on a leaf.
Up-set, down-set, common requirements Yes. No. Through rules over three features, two selections together can force more.
Rebuilt feature tree No. A proposal: one of several possible trees. No. No groups, no abstract features.
False-optional features Yes. Yes when the parent is in the graphs; no when it is abstract.
Tree agreement, redundant constraints Yes, for chains of requirements. No. Redundancy through rules over three features is not seen; a candidate needs a solver to confirm.
Whole-model numbers (vp_summary) Yes. Exact on the graphs. No. They describe the graphs, not the model.
Consistency checks (vp_check) Yes. No. The files against each other, not against the model.
Degree distribution, Gini Yes. Exact on the graphs. No. How concentrated, not which features nor whether it is good; the complete graph has long tails by construction.
Primitive conflicts Yes. No. Whether one was written or follows from a longer rule needs the model.
Explanations (vp_explain_*) Yes. Every step is a true relationship. No. Links of the graphs, not constraints of the model.
Groups of alternatives, colouring, largest compatible set Yes. The groups are true; the largest set is a true ceiling. No. “At least one” groups are not in the graphs; the colouring and, for large models, the largest set are not always the best.
Twins Yes, for the graphs. No. A rule over three features can tell twins apart.
Candidate groups, conflict cover Yes. Every group is “at most one”. No. “Exactly one” groups are not seen; the cover is small, not always the smallest.
Opposites, primitive at-least-one lines, requirements from conflicts Yes. Yes for pairs, with the at-least-one graph.
Two features (vp_pair) Yes. Yes, with the at-least-one graph: exact.
Wish lists, partial configurations: a FALSE Yes. Always right. No. Misses what only a rule over three features forbids.
Wish lists, partial configurations: a TRUE No. A rule over three features can forbid it (One rule, three features, and every function). Yes. Every possible list gets a TRUE.
Consequences of decisions Yes. No. Decisions together can force more than each alone.
Kernel (vp_kernel) Yes for its “no”; its “yes” can be wrong. No. What follows from leaving features out is not in it.
Safe order (vp_rounds) Yes, for requirements between two features. No. A conflict within a round, or a rule over three features, can still make a later answer impossible.
Modal implication graph (vp_mig) Yes. No. Implications between two decisions only: the strong arrows of a MIG, never the weak ones.
Independent parts, cut features Yes, for relationships between two features. No. Rules over three features can tie parts together.
Links between teams, team summaries (vp_team_links, vp_teams) Yes. Each link is a true interference. No. Two teams can interfere through a rule over three features with no link between them.
Moving features between teams Yes, the counts. No. A candidate for a person: who knows a feature matters more.
A split proposed by the links Yes, the counts. No. It knows links, not people; it depends on the seed.
Order of the teams (vp_team_order) Yes, for requirements between two features. No. Conflicts need agreement in any order; rules over three features can still undo an earlier decision.
Decisions that cut the model (vp_split_after, vp_splitting_decisions) Yes, for relationships between two features. No. Rules over three features can tie the parts left; only single decisions are searched.
Combinations to cover Yes. Yes, with the at-least-one graph; an upper limit without it.
Coverage of a sample Yes. Yes for combinations of one or two features.
Sample violations Yes. Each one breaks a true relationship. No. A configuration can be invalid and break no link.
Lower bound on the sample size Yes. No covering sample is smaller. No. The true minimum can be larger.
Triangles, communities, robustness, coreness Yes, on the graphs (communities depend on the seed). No. Patterns of pairs only.
Power law, baseline Statistical answers, with a margin of error. No. They depend on the test and on the randomisation; the baseline covers dependencies only.
Features that look alike Yes, the similarities. No. They raise questions; only whoever maintains the model knows the answer.
Comparing versions Yes. What it reports did change. No. Invisible: changes that touch only rules over three features, and renames.
Drawing changes (vp_plot_compare) Yes, but a “lost” arrow of the minimal form can be one that became implied. No. As comparing versions.
Ripple Yes, for written changes as the minimal form approximates them. No. Changes of rules over three features ripple invisibly.
Interaction changes (vp_interaction_changes) Yes. Exact for two kept features (property P3). Yes for pairs of kept features; no for features that changed state, or for rules over three.
Rename candidates No. Candidates for a person to confirm. No. A rename with changed links can be missed; a feature with no link to the kept ones cannot be matched.
Sizes, changes, shape over time (vp_history_apply) Yes, on the graphs of each version. No. Each measure keeps its own limits; features added or removed can look like a trend.
Growth laws Yes, the fitted line. No. A power law is assumed; three points give a slope, not a trustworthy one.
Type of each step No. Only “arbitrary edit” is certain; the others are possible. No. Necessary conditions only.
Hubs, disruptions Yes, on the graphs of the history. No. Judged against the same history; the threshold is a convention.
Version distances, eras Yes, on the kept features of each pair. No. Versions sharing few features look alike; the number of eras is a choice.
Communities over time Yes, next to two runs on one version. No. The randomness of the algorithm can be as large as the change.
Attachment, churn, co-change Yes, on the graphs of the history. No. Changes of rules over three features count for nothing; a co-change is a candidate, not a dependency.
Link lifetimes, life cycle Yes, on the graphs of the history. No. Few cases in a calm history; all steps pooled.
Flips No. Candidates: a rename looks like a flip. No. As the states of the features.
Predictions Estimates, with their error measured on later versions. No. The causes of change are mostly outside the graphs.
Representativeness (vp_representativeness) Yes. Exact counts by GANAK. Yes for whole configurations of the formula; it says nothing about wish lists, nor about what the formula leaves out of a UVL model.
Counting by trying every configuration (vp_count_graph_products) Yes. Exact. Yes, up to 20 features.

What a high measure means, and what a low one does not

The measures of Measuring each feature to Patterns and statistics rank features: by how many features require them, by how many chains pass through them, by how much selecting them decides. How far can a ranking be trusted?

A high value is real. Every arrow counted by required_by is a relationship that holds in every valid configuration. If 1,764 options of Linux require NET, then 1,764 options cannot be selected without it: changing NET affects them all, whatever else the model says. The same holds for betweenness (each chain it counts is made of true requirements) and for decision_power (each feature it counts is truly decided). So a feature that ranks high is important. (It may borrow its importance from another one: Genuine hubs.)

A low value is not proof of unimportance. The graphs hold relationships between two features. A feature can be important through rules over three or more features, and those leave no arrow. The band has an example:

vp_feature_table(band) |>
  filter(feature %in% c("BLEv40", "BLEv42")) |>
  select(feature, required_by, betweenness)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>   feature required_by betweenness
#>   <chr>         <int>       <dbl>
#> 1 BLEv40            1           1
#> 2 BLEv42            0           0
with_screen <- products |> filter(Screen == 1) # the bands with a screen
mean(with_screen$BLEv40 == 1 | with_screen$BLEv42 == 1)
#> [1] 1
# 1: every one of them has one of the two versions

BLEv42 is required by no feature, and BLEv40 by one. Judged one by one, they look marginal. Yet every band with a screen (18 of the 24) has one of the two: the rule “a band with BLE has version 4.0 or 4.2” makes the pair indispensable, and no arrow points to either. In Linux every depends on A || B does the same: A and B each look unrequired, while together they are needed. The same blind spot affects every measure: a chain that runs through such a rule is no chain of the graphs, so it adds to nobody’s betweenness.

So use the measures to find important features, never to declare a feature unimportant. Before deciding that a feature with low values can be removed or ignored, look for it in the rules of the model that tie three or more features; representativeness (How much the graphs leave out: representativeness) says how much of the model such rules hold.

Everything the functions of the vignettes compute from the graphs is true of the graphs, and every relationship in the graphs is true of the model. What is missing is the rules over three or more features. When an answer matters (a “yes” to a long wish list, “nothing changed” between two versions), check it against the model with a solver.

What the graphs cannot see

The rest of this vignette is about the most important thing to know about the results of variplex: everything they say is true, but they do not say everything. Two things are missing from them. The graphs hold relationships between two features, and a model can have rules that tie three or more features at once (A rule that no pair can show). And for a UVL model, the formula itself can leave out part of the model: its numbers and texts, and how many copies a feature with a cardinality has (Features that are more than yes or no). Why it is true: a proof proves all of this.

A rule that no pair can show

Here is the smallest example. A band has three optional features and one rule: the battery cannot power the three at once.

tiny_file <- vp_example("tiny_band.uvl")
cat(readLines(tiny_file), sep = "\n")
#> features
#>  TinyBand {abstract true}
#>      optional
#>          GPS
#>          NFC
#>          AlwaysOnDisplay
#> 
#> constraints
#>  !(GPS & NFC & AlwaysOnDisplay)
GPS NFC AlwaysOnDisplay
yes yes yes not valid
yes yes – valid
yes – yes valid
yes – – valid
– yes yes valid
– yes – valid
– – yes valid
– – – valid

Now look at the features two by two. GPS and NFC can go together; so can GPS and AlwaysOnDisplay, and NFC and AlwaysOnDisplay. No feature requires another, no two exclude each other, and none of the three is needed. There is no relationship between two features at all, and variplex says exactly that:

tiny <- vp_generate(tiny_file, or_graph = TRUE)
tiny
#> variplex model "tiny_band"
#>   features: 3 variable (the nodes of the graphs), 0 core, 0 dead
#>   requires: 0 arrows   excludes: 0 lines
#>   at least one: 0 lines
#>   atomic sets: 0 (of two or more features)
vp_pair(tiny, "GPS", "NFC")
#> # A tibble: 4 x 5
#>   combination a     b     possible ruled_out_by
#>   <chr>       <lgl> <lgl> <lgl>    <chr>       
#> 1 both        TRUE  TRUE  TRUE     ""          
#> 2 only GPS    TRUE  FALSE TRUE     ""          
#> 3 only NFC    FALSE TRUE  TRUE     ""          
#> 4 neither     FALSE FALSE TRUE     ""
The rule of the tiny band ties three features at once. The graphs join features two by two, and here they have nothing to join.

The rule is not lost: it is in the model, and every valid configuration respects it. It is simply not a relationship between two features, so no graph of pairs can hold it. Rules of this kind are common: “a feature needs one of two others” (A => B | C), “these three cannot go together”, and the groups of a feature diagram, “at least one of these children”. Some representations also keep such rules, like the modal implication graphs used to propagate configuration decisions Krieter et al. (2018); the graphs of variplex keep the plain meaning of an arrow instead.

What is always true, and what may be missing

The table goes through every result, for what is in the formula (Features that are more than yes or no is about what the formula leaves out).

Result Is what it says true? Does it say everything?
Core and dead features Yes. Each core feature is in every valid configuration, and each dead feature in none. Yes. Every core and every dead feature is found.
The three graphs: requires, excludes, at least one Yes. Every arrow and every line holds in every valid configuration. No. They hold every relationship between two features, but the rules over three or more features are in none of them.
Atomic sets Yes. The features of an atomic set are always selected together. Yes. Every group of features that are always selected together is found.
Minimal form Yes. It is the graphs without repetitions. No. It says what the graphs say (vp_expand() gives them back), and no more.
Kernel: its boxes, arrows and red lines Yes. Each arrow and each red line is a true relationship between boxes. No. It keeps only what the graphs say about “can these go together?”.
Kernel: a “no” to a wish list Yes. Two of the features, or two features that they bring along, exclude each other in every valid configuration. No. It misses the wish lists that only a rule over three or more features forbids.
Kernel: a “yes” to a wish list No. A rule over three or more features can still forbid the list (How representative are the graphs? measures how often). Yes. Every wish list that can be built gets a “yes”.
Explanations (vp_explain_conflict(), vp_explain_requires()) Yes. Every step of a chain is a true relationship. No. It answers with the links of the graphs, not with the rules of the model that made them.
Comparing versions (vp_compare()) Yes. What it reports did change. No. A change that only touches a rule over three or more features is invisible to it.
Which variables are features (__variables.csv), for a UVL model Yes. variplex translated the model itself and marked its helper variables. Yes. Every variable is listed, with its class and the rule that decided (The two reports: what was decided, and how the run went).
Which variables are features, for a formula made by another tool No. Not always: it is decided by rules on the names, which an unusual name can fool. Yes. Every variable is listed, with its class and the rule that decided, so a wrong decision can be found.

An example of the row of the explanations. In the Mi Band 3, BLEv42 requires HeartRateSensor, and the explanation is a single arrow:

vp_explain_requires(band, "BLEv42", "HeartRateSensor")
#> # A tibble: 1 x 5
#>   route  step from   link     to             
#>   <int> <int> <chr>  <chr>    <chr>          
#> 1     1     1 BLEv42 requires HeartRateSensor

No constraint of the model says so. It follows from BLE => HeartRateSensor | MovementFilter, a rule over three features, together with the fact that the movement filter needs BLE version 4.0. The graphs keep what the rule implies for pairs, and only that.

The kernel: a “no” is final, a “yes” is a good guess

On the tiny band the kernel has a single class, “can always be added”, with the three features:

vp_kernel(tiny)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 4
#>   class label feature         trouble_free
#>   <int> <chr> <chr>           <lgl>       
#> 1     1 GPS   GPS             TRUE        
#> 2     1 GPS   NFC             TRUE        
#> 3     1 GPS   AlwaysOnDisplay TRUE

So the kernel answers “yes” to the wish list “GPS, NFC and AlwaysOnDisplay”, which no valid configuration has.

The same happens on the Mi Band 3. Add the rule of the tiny band to it, now for NFC, the heart-rate sensor and the touch screen:

tail(readLines(vp_example("miband3_battery.uvl")), 1)
#> [1] "\t!(NFC & HeartRateSensor & TouchScreen)"
identical(vp_kernel(battery), vp_kernel(band))
#> [1] TRUE

Every pair of the three is still possible, so no relationship between two features changes, and the kernel of the new model is the kernel of the band: But the model has lost 4 of its 24 valid configurations, and the wish lists that can be built drop from 520 to 424. The kernel still says “yes” to 520: it is wrong 96 times. The smallest wrong answers are 4 wish lists of three features: BLEv42, ContactlessPayment, TouchScreen; BLEv42, NFC, TouchScreen; ContactlessPayment, HeartRateSensor, TouchScreen; HeartRateSensor, NFC, TouchScreen (contactless payment brings NFC along, and Bluetooth 4.2 brings the heart-rate sensor). Among them is the first wish list of The kernel: “can these go together?”, which was buildable before the battery rule.

Why is a “no” always right? The kernel says “no” when two of the features you want, or two of the features they bring along, exclude each other, and that holds in every valid configuration. A “yes” only means that no two features stand in each other’s way; a rule over three or more features can still forbid the whole list. That is why the help of vp_kernel() and vp_can_go_together() says so.

Comparisons cannot see it either

Compare the Mi Band 3 with the same band plus the battery rule:

vp_compare(band, battery)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 10
#>   graph       kept added removed old_links new_links gained  lost jaccard spearman
#>   <chr>      <int> <int>   <int>     <int>     <int>  <int> <int>   <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 requires      11     0       0        21        21      0     0       1        1
#> 2 excludes      11     0       0        10        10      0     0       1       NA
#> 3 atleastone    11     0       0         3         3      0     0       1       NA

No change at all, and Jaccard 1 everywhere, while the model lost 4 of its 24 products. A comparison of the graphs compares relationships between two features, and none of them changed.

How representative are the graphs?

The graphs can be wrong in one way only: they can let pass a combination of features that the model forbids. Every link they hold is true, so a combination that breaks one of them is impossible. How representative the graphs are is therefore one question: of the combinations that the graphs let pass, how many are really possible? It has two versions, for two kinds of combination: whole products, and wish lists.

Whole products

Choose, for every feature that can vary, whether a product has it. The graphs let the choice pass when it breaks none of their links: no arrow goes from a chosen feature to one left out, no red line joins two chosen features, and no green line joins two features left out. On the Mi Band 3, 42 choices pass, and 24 of them are valid configurations: 57 %. The smallest choice that passes and is not valid is a band with CapacityButton, OLED, Screen and none of the other features that can vary. It breaks no link, but it has a screen, so it has BLE (the abstract feature that the graphs leave out), and no BLE version, while the model says that a band with BLE has one of the versions BLEv40 and BLEv42: a rule over three features. (It also lacks the heart-rate sensor or the movement filter that constraint 2 asks of a band with BLE, another rule over three features.)

Wish lists

A wish list only says what a product must have, and the graphs let it pass when no red line joins two of its features: exactly the question of the kernel, which gives the same answers. For wish lists the Mi Band 3 is perfectly represented: every wish list that the graphs let pass can be built. The rule about the BLE versions does not matter for a wish list, because a band with BLE can always take one of the versions.

Both measures were taken for every model of the vignettes that is small enough to try every combination:

Model Features that vary Whole products: let pass valid share Wish lists: right “yes”
Mi Band 1 0 1 1 100 % 100 %
Mi Band 1s 1 2 2 100 % 100 %
Mi Band 2 8 32 24 75 % 100 %
Mi Band 3 11 42 24 57 % 100 %
Mi Band 4 17 140 72 51 % 100 %
Mi Band 6 21 42 22 52 % 100 %
Mi Band 8 23 43 21 49 % 100 %
Mi Band 3 with the battery rule 11 42 20 48 % 82 %
The tiny band (Section A rule that no pair can show) 3 8 7 88 % 88 %

The graphs of every Mi Band answer wish lists perfectly, while about half of the whole products they let pass are not valid (49 % of them are, at worst). Rules like “a band with BLE has one of the versions” are common in feature models, because every group with an “or” or an “alternative” is one; they matter when a whole product is decided, and rarely when a wish list is. The battery rule is different: it forbids a wish list, so it lowers both measures.

Measuring your own model

For whole products the measure is a ratio of two counts, and the option representativeness = TRUE computes it: share=products of the model, counted over the features of the graphschoices of the same features that the graphs let pass.\text{share} = \frac{\text{products of the model, counted over the features of the graphs}}{\text{choices of the same features that the graphs let pass}} . Counting the products of a model one by one is hopeless beyond a few dozen features that vary, and a SAT solver, which answers “is there one?”, does not help. The tool for it is a model counter, or #SAT solver: it counts the solutions of a formula without listing them, by splitting it into parts that share no variable and remembering the parts it has already counted Sundermann et al. (2021). variplex uses GANAK (https://github.com/meelgroup/ganak), an exact model counter: in the Model Counting Competition 2024 it solved the most formulas with exact counts in all four tracks, among them plain and projected model counting (https://mccompetition.org/assets/files/2024/MC2024_awards.pdf). It is a separate program: download it from the releases of its page (there are programs for Linux, macOS and Windows) and put it on the PATH, or give its path with the argument ganak of vp_generate().

variplex gives GANAK two formulas, and keeps them with the other files of the run:

  • __count_formula.cnf, the formula of the model, headed by a line c p show with the variables of the features in the graphs. GANAK then counts the choices of those features that some configuration has, and not the configurations themselves: a configuration also sets the abstract features and the helper variables of the translation, which are not in the graphs. This is a projected count.

  • __count_graphs.cnf, the graphs written as a formula: one variable for each feature of the graphs, and one clause for each link. An arrow a→ba \to b is the clause ¬a∨b\lnot a \lor b, a red line aa — bb is ¬a∨¬b\lnot a \lor \lnot b, and a green line is a∨ba \lor b (Why it is true: a proof). Its solutions are the choices that the graphs let pass, which is why the option also computes the third graph.

On the Mi Band 3 with the battery rule:

vp_representativeness(battery)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 5
#>   vm_configurations graph_configurations share left_out note 
#>               <dbl>                <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl> <chr>
#> 1                20                   42 0.476    0.524 ""
str(battery$summary$representativeness)
#> List of 5
#>  $ counter       : chr "/home/rheradio/s4vm_work/tools/ganak/ganak"
#>  $ configurations: chr "20"
#>  $ graph_choices : chr "42"
#>  $ share         : num 0.476
#>  $ left_out      : num 0.524

20 of the 42 choices that the graphs let pass are products: 47.6 %, the share of the table above, found this time without trying a single combination. The summary keeps the two counts as text, because on a large model they have more digits than any integer of a program can hold, and adds left_out, the share that the graphs leave out. If GANAK cannot count, the graphs are still written, the summary says why, and vp_representativeness() gives the reason in note.

Counting works for large models too: Each count took less than a second here, but counting is harder than the questions that make the graphs, and a formula of thousands of variables can take GANAK much longer.

Model let pass products share
Mi Band 3 42 24 57.1 %
Mi Band 3 with the battery rule 42 20 47.6 %
uClibc 1.08 × 1042 1.66 × 1040 1.5 %
BusyBox 1.18.0 1.99 × 10208 1.89 × 10207 9.5 %

For uClibc, 1.5 % of the whole products that the graphs let pass are products, and for BusyBox 1.18.0, 9.5 %: for whole products, the graphs of a large model are a loose approximation. Wish lists are another matter, as the next section shows: the share of the wish lists that the graphs let pass and that can be built stays high, because a wish list leaves the other features free. To be sure about one wish list, ask the solver (How to be sure).

The graphs are fully representative of the wish lists of a model when every wish list that cannot be built contains two features that cannot go together, and of its whole products when every rule of the model can be written as relationships between two features. Measure them on your model before you trust a “yes” for a long wish list or for a whole product.

In real models

Is this a curiosity, or a daily problem? Two measurements on real models.

Most clauses are about two features. A formula is a list of clauses, and a clause with two literals is a relationship between two variables. In the 5,709 formulas of the dataset of Strong4VM, with 199,787,155 clauses in all, 60% of the clauses have two literals, and in 75% of the formulas more than half of them do (the table below). Formulas translated from feature models (TraVarT) are almost all pairs; formulas made by KConfigReader are not, because of the way it encodes Kconfig.

Translator Formulas Clauses 1 literal 2 literals 3 literals 4 or more
KMax 2,058 65,078,833 16 % 62 % 9 % 13 %
KConfigReader 1,340 69,144,889 5 % 24 % 39 % 32 %
KconfigSampler 5 14,178 10 % 66 % 25 % 0 %
TraVarT 2,306 65,549,255 0 % 98 % 1 % 1 %
All 5,709 199,787,155 7 % 60 % 17 % 16 %

So a formula is mostly a large web of pairs, plus some longer rules, which is why the graphs show most of what matters. But the share of pairs does not tell how often the graphs are wrong: one longer rule can be enough to fool them (the battery rule), and many longer rules can be harmless (KConfigReader). That needs the second measurement.

For wish lists, the graphs are rarely wrong, but they can be. For each of the seven Mi Bands, every wish list was checked against the valid configurations, up to 8,388,608 of them for the Mi Band 8: the graphs, and the kernel, were never wrong. On 10 large real models, 1,000 random wish lists that the graphs let pass were drawn for each size, and a SAT solver checked whether they can be built (wish lists of two features, the control, were never wrong). The table gives, for each size of wish list, how many of the 1,000 wish lists that the graphs let pass cannot be built:

Model Translator Options 3 5 10 20 50
Linux x86 3.13 KMax 7,100 0 0 0 0 20
Linux x86 2.6.24 KMax 3,612 0 0 1 5 21
Linux x86 2.6.24 KConfigReader 3,579 0 0 0 0 2
Linux S390 2.5.45 KConfigReader 425 0 0 0 0 0
BusyBox 1.33.0 KconfigSampler 1,003 0 0 0 0 0
Automotive01 TraVarT 2,199 0 0 0 3 17
Automotive2 2.4 TraVarT 16,829 0 0 0 0 0
BusyBox 1.18.0 UVL 819 0 0 0 0 0
axTLS UVL 61 0 0 0 0 0
uClibc UVL 238 1 3 17 111 429

In 9 of the 10 models the graphs were never wrong for wish lists of up to 5 features, wrong for at most 0.1% of those of 10, and for at most 2.1% of those of 50. uClibc is the exception: 0.1% of the wish lists of 3 features, 1.7% of those of 10 and 43% of those of 50. Its constraints are full of rules over many options. One of them says that USE_BX needs an ARM target or a Cortex-M processor; so USE_BX, the VAX target (which excludes the ARM target) and the ARM10T processor (which excludes both Cortex-M processors) pass every pair test, and cannot be built together.

The graphs and the kernel are a good approximation of the model: what they say is true, and they are rarely wrong when they let a wish list pass. But an approximation is all they are, and how good it is depends on the model, on the size of the question, and on whether it is about a wish list or a whole product.

How to be sure

When the answer matters, ask the solver. variplex itself can do it: write the wish list as one more constraint of the model, and run it. If no valid configuration has all the wished features, the model has no product left, and vp_generate() stops with an error of class variplex_void_model (A model without any product):

tail(readLines(vp_example("miband3_battery_wish.uvl")), 2)
#> [1] "\t!(NFC & HeartRateSensor & TouchScreen)" "\tTouchScreen & HeartRateSensor & NFC"
e <- tryCatch(
  vp_generate(vp_example("miband3_battery_wish.uvl")),
  error = function(e) e
)
class(e)
#> [1] "variplex_void_model" "variplex_error"      "error"               "condition"
inherits(vp_generate(vp_example("miband3_wish.uvl")), "vp_model")
#> [1] TRUE

The first model is the Mi Band 3 with the battery rule: the wish list cannot be built. The second is the Mi Band 3 as it is: it can. The solver only knows what is in the formula: a constraint that variplex leaves out of a UVL model (What the formula leaves out: numbers and texts) is left out of this check too. For such a model, use a tool that understands numbers, such as an SMT solver.

Features that are more than yes or no

Up to here every feature was something that a product has or does not have. variplex works on a logic formula, whose variables are true or false, so that is all it can take from a model. UVL, the Universal Variability Language, now says much more. Its web page1 sorts what it can say into three language levels:

  • Boolean: the feature tree, the groups (also with a group cardinality, such as [0..2]: from none to two of the children), and constraints between features (NFC => GPS).

  • Arithmetic: attributes, numbers attached to a feature (GPS {power 30}); constraints that compute with them (GPS.power + NFC.power < 50), also over all the selected features at once (sum(power) < 80, or avg); and feature cardinality, a feature that a product can have several times (Strap cardinality [1..2]: one strap or two).

  • Type: features with a value, Integer, Real or String (Integer BatteryCapacity), and constraints on those values, with functions such as floor, ceil and len, the length of a text.

Two more things fit in no level: a constraint can be written inside the attributes of a feature (Screen {constraint Screen => Touch}), and a model can import the features of another model (imports). This chapter tells what vp_generate() does with each of them, what that means for every result, and what you can do about it.

What variplex does with each

Here is a band that uses them all:

cat(readLines(vp_example("uvl_tour.uvl")), sep = "\n")
#> features
#>  Band {abstract true}
#>      mandatory
#>          Integer BatteryCapacity
#>          Real Price
#>          String Model
#>          Strap cardinality [1..2]
#>      optional
#>          Screen {power 40, constraint Screen => Touch}
#>              optional
#>                  Touch {power 5}
#>          GPS {power 30}
#>          NFC {power 10}
#> 
#> constraints
#>  NFC => GPS
#>  sum(power) < 80
#>  GPS.power + NFC.power < 50
#>  BatteryCapacity > 100
#>  floor(Price) < 100
#>  len(Model) < 20

And here is what vp_generate() says about it:

tour <- vp_generate(vp_example("uvl_tour.uvl"))
#> Warning: uvl_tour.uvl: line 17: constraint "sum(power) < 80"
#> was skipped: it could not be parsed (it likely contains unsupported constructs such as aggregate
#> functions, attribute access, or typed feature references)
#> Warning: uvl_tour.uvl: line 20: constraint "floor(Price) <
#> 100" was skipped: it could not be parsed (it likely contains unsupported constructs such as
#> aggregate functions, attribute access, or typed feature references)
#> Warning: uvl_tour.uvl: line 21: constraint "len(Model) < 20"
#> was skipped: it could not be parsed (it likely contains unsupported constructs such as aggregate
#> functions, attribute access, or typed feature references)
#> Warning: uvl_tour.uvl: line 18: constraint "GPS.power +
#> NFC.power < 50" was skipped: it is not purely Boolean (arithmetic or comparison)
#> Warning: uvl_tour.uvl: line 19: constraint "BatteryCapacity >
#> 100" was skipped: it is not purely Boolean (arithmetic or comparison)
#> Warning: uvl_tour.uvl: line 7: feature "Strap" has the
#> feature cardinality [1..2]: it is encoded as one feature, mandatory or optional as its group says;
#> the number of its copies, and what each copy has, are not represented.
#> Warning: uvl_tour.uvl: 3 feature(s) are declared Integer,
#> String or Real; they are encoded only by their presence, their values are not represented
#> (R-UVL-06).

It names the 5 constraints that it leaves out, counts the 3 features with a value, and warns that Strap has a feature cardinality: it becomes one mandatory feature, and therefore a core feature. The constraint in the attributes of Screen is read like any other, so in the graphs the screen requires the touch layer. The table goes through every construct.

|:—————————————————|:—————————————–|:—————————————————————————————————————————————|:————————————————-| | Construct | Example | What variplex does | Does it tell you? | | Feature tree, groups, constraints between features | NFC => GPS | Translates them exactly. | — | | Group cardinality | [0..2] | Translates it exactly. | — | | Attribute | GPS {power 30} | Sets it aside: it is a number, not a feature. | Through the constraints that use it (next rows). | | Arithmetic on attributes | GPS.power + NFC.power < 50 | Leaves the constraint out. | Yes, with its line. | | Aggregate | sum(power) < 80 | Leaves the constraint out. | Yes, with its line. | | Feature with a value | Integer BatteryCapacity | Keeps the feature: whether a product has it, not its value. | Yes, how many there are. | | Constraint on a value | BatteryCapacity > 100, floor(Price) < 100, len(Model) < 20 | Leaves the constraint out. | Yes, with its line. | | Feature cardinality | Strap cardinality [1..2] | Keeps one feature, mandatory or optional as its group says; how many copies a product has, and what each copy has, is not represented. | Yes, with its line. | | Constraint written as an attribute | Screen {constraint Screen => Touch} | Reads it like the constraints of the section constraints: translates it when it is Boolean, leaves it out when it is not. | Yes, when it leaves it out. | | Imported model | imports sensors.Pack as S | Does not read the imported features, and leaves out every constraint that names one. | Yes, for each constraint. |

What the formula leaves out: numbers and texts

A logic formula cannot hold numbers or texts, so a constraint that computes with them is left out. Here is the tiny band of A rule that no pair can show again, its rule written this time with numbers, and with a battery whose capacity is a number:

cat(readLines(vp_example("numbers_band.uvl")), sep = "\n")
#> features
#>  TinyBand {abstract true}
#>      mandatory
#>          Integer BatteryCapacity
#>      optional
#>          GPS {power 30}
#>          NFC {power 10}
#>          AlwaysOnDisplay {power 25}
#> 
#> constraints
#>  GPS.power + NFC.power + AlwaysOnDisplay.power < 60
#>  BatteryCapacity > 100

The constraint on the power says what the battery rule of A rule that no pair can show said: any two of the three features draw less than 60, and the three together draw 65. variplex warns about every constraint that it leaves out, and about every feature with a type:

numbers <- vp_generate(vp_example("numbers_band.uvl"))
#> Warning: numbers_band.uvl: line 11: constraint "GPS.power +
#> NFC.power + AlwaysOnDisplay.power < 60" was skipped: it is not purely Boolean (arithmetic or
#> comparison)
#> Warning: numbers_band.uvl: line 12: constraint
#> "BatteryCapacity > 100" was skipped: it is not purely Boolean (arithmetic or comparison)
#> Warning: numbers_band.uvl: 1 feature(s) are declared Integer,
#> String or Real; they are encoded only by their presence, their values are not represented
#> (R-UVL-06).
numbers
#> variplex model "numbers_band"
#>   features: 3 variable (the nodes of the graphs), 1 core, 0 dead
#>   requires: 0 arrows   excludes: 0 lines
#>   at least one: not computed (use vp_generate(or_graph = TRUE))
#>   atomic sets: 0 (of two or more features)

The rule is gone, and this time not only from the graphs: it is not even in the formula, so the formula allows all eight combinations of the three features. The summary counts what was left out, under uvl, and strict_uvl = TRUE turns a constraint left out into an error:

numbers$summary$uvl[c("skipped_constraints", "typed_features")]
#> $skipped_constraints
#> [1] 2
#> 
#> $typed_features
#> [1] 1
e <- tryCatch(
  suppressWarnings(vp_generate(
    vp_example("numbers_band.uvl"),
    strict_uvl = TRUE
  )),
  error = function(e) e
)
class(e)
#> [1] "variplex_strict_uvl" "variplex_error"      "error"               "condition"

strict_uvl = TRUE stops for every constraint left out, also one written as an attribute. It does not stop for a feature with a value, nor for a feature cardinality: neither leaves a constraint out, though both leave something unsaid.

Even two features

In What is always true, and what may be missing the graphs missed only rules over three or more features: every relationship between two features was found, and every core and dead feature. That was because the formula held the whole model. When the formula leaves something out, it allows more than the model does, and then even those can be missed. A band with a power budget:

cat(readLines(vp_example("power_band.uvl")), sep = "\n")
#> features
#>  PowerBand {abstract true}
#>      optional
#>          Screen {power 40}
#>              optional
#>                  AlwaysOnDisplay {power 25}
#>                  Projector {power 45}
#>          GPS {power 30}
#>          NFC {power 10}
#> 
#> constraints
#>  sum(power) < 80

The screen with the always-on display and the GPS draws 95, over the budget of 80, and the screen with the projector draws 85. So in the model AlwaysOnDisplay and GPS exclude each other, and Projector is dead: no band can have it. The formula holds only the tree, which allows 20 configurations; with its budget, the model has 9. variplex sees the tree:

power <- vp_generate(vp_example("power_band.uvl"), or_graph = TRUE)
#> Warning: power_band.uvl: line 12: constraint "sum(power) <
#> 80" was skipped: it could not be parsed (it likely contains unsupported constructs such as
#> aggregate functions, attribute access, or typed feature references)
vp_links(power, "requires")
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>   from            to    
#>   <chr>           <chr> 
#> 1 AlwaysOnDisplay Screen
#> 2 Projector       Screen
vp_features(power)
#> # A tibble: 5 x 2
#>   feature         status  
#>   <chr>           <chr>   
#> 1 Screen          variable
#> 2 AlwaysOnDisplay variable
#> 3 Projector       variable
#> 4 GPS             variable
#> 5 NFC             variable

Its two arrows are true: AlwaysOnDisplay and Projector require Screen (for the projector it holds because no band has one). But there is no red line between AlwaysOnDisplay and GPS, and Projector is shown as a feature that can vary. At the extreme, the numbers can rule out every product:

cat(readLines(vp_example("void_numbers.uvl")), sep = "\n")
#> features
#>  Band {abstract true}
#>      mandatory
#>          Integer BatteryCapacity
#>      optional
#>          GPS
#> 
#> constraints
#>  BatteryCapacity > 200
#>  BatteryCapacity < 150
vp_generate(vp_example("void_numbers.uvl"))
#> Warning: void_numbers.uvl: line 9: constraint
#> "BatteryCapacity > 200" was skipped: it is not purely Boolean (arithmetic or comparison)
#> Warning: void_numbers.uvl: line 10: constraint
#> "BatteryCapacity < 150" was skipped: it is not purely Boolean (arithmetic or comparison)
#> Warning: void_numbers.uvl: 1 feature(s) are declared Integer,
#> String or Real; they are encoded only by their presence, their values are not represented
#> (R-UVL-06).
#> variplex model "void_numbers"
#>   features: 1 variable (the nodes of the graphs), 1 core, 0 dead
#>   requires: 0 arrows   excludes: 0 lines
#>   at least one: not computed (use vp_generate(or_graph = TRUE))
#>   atomic sets: 0 (of two or more features)

No battery has more than 200 and less than 150, so this model has no valid configuration. variplex finds one feature that can vary and no error, not the error of a model without products (A model without any product).

What is always true, and what may be missing, with numbers

This is the table of What is always true, and what may be missing again, for a model whose formula leaves something out. The first column hardly changes: leaving a constraint out only removes restrictions, so what holds in every configuration of the formula holds in every configuration of the model. The second column changes everywhere: almost nothing is complete any more.

Result Is what it says true? Does it say everything?
A model without valid configurations (an error) Yes. When the formula has no configuration, neither has the model. No. A model that only its numbers leave without products is analysed as if it had some.
Core and dead features Yes. No. A feature that the numbers make core or dead is shown as one that can vary (Projector).
The three graphs: requires, excludes, at least one Yes. Every arrow and every line holds in every valid configuration. No. The relationships that come from the numbers are missing, also those between two features (AlwaysOnDisplay and GPS).
Atomic sets Yes. No. Features that only the numbers keep together are not grouped.
Minimal form Yes. No. It says what the graphs say.
Kernel: its boxes, arrows and red lines Yes. No. It keeps what the graphs say about “can these go together?”.
Kernel: a “no” to a wish list Yes. No. It misses the wish lists that the numbers forbid, even of two features.
Kernel: a “yes” to a wish list No. The numbers can forbid the list, even a list of two features (AlwaysOnDisplay and GPS). Yes.
Explanations Yes. No. It cannot point at a constraint that the formula left out.
Comparing versions Yes. No. A change of a number, such as a new budget, is invisible to it.
A feature with a value (Integer, Real, String) Yes, about whether a product has it. No. Its value is not represented.
A feature with a cardinality Yes, about whether a product has it. No. How many copies a product has, and what each copy has, is not represented; variplex warns.
A constraint written as an attribute Yes. It is read like any other constraint. Yes, when it is Boolean; when it is not, it is left out, with a warning, like any other.
Which variables are features (__variables.csv) Yes. Yes. Every feature is listed, also those with a value, which the summary counts.

With numbers, a “yes”, a “no”, a red line or an arrow from variplex is still true. What changes is that its silence means less: a missing line, a feature shown as variable or a model with products may only be the effect of a number that the formula left out.

What you can do

  • Read the warnings. Each constraint left out is named with its line, each feature cardinality too, the summary counts them, and strict_uvl = TRUE refuses a model that leaves a constraint out.

  • Write fixed numbers as rules. An attribute is a fixed number, so a constraint on attributes, like the power budget, forbids certain combinations of features, and those can be written as constraints between features. For the band with the power budget, the 3 smallest combinations over the budget are:

tail(readLines(vp_example("power_band_boolean.uvl")), 3)
#> [1] "\t!(Screen & Projector)"             "\t!(Screen & AlwaysOnDisplay & GPS)"
#> [3] "\t!(Screen & GPS & NFC)"
With them, the graphs hold everything that the budget does to two features: *Projector* is dead, and *AlwaysOnDisplay* and *GPS* exclude each other. The third rule ties three features (80 is not below 80), so no graph can hold it ([A rule that no pair can show](#sec:pairs)).
power_boolean <- vp_generate(
  vp_example("power_band_boolean.uvl"),
  or_graph = TRUE
)
vp_links(power_boolean, "excludes")
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>   from            to   
#>   <chr>           <chr>
#> 1 AlwaysOnDisplay GPS
vp_features(power_boolean) |> filter(status == "dead")
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>   feature   status
#>   <chr>     <chr> 
#> 1 Projector dead

  • Turn a value into features. When only a few values of a feature matter, a feature for each range can stand for them: a feature LargeBattery for a capacity over 100, with the constraints written on it.

  • Turn copies into features. When the number of copies matters, the copies can be features of their own (Strap1, Strap2), in a group with a cardinality.

  • Ask a tool that understands numbers. For the rest, a solver of formulas with numbers, an SMT solver, can answer what vp_generate() cannot.

Why it is true: a proof

The tables of What is always true, and what may be missing and What is always true, and what may be missing, with numbers make two kinds of claim: what vp_generate() says is true, and what it says about one or two features is complete. This section proves both. The idea fits in a line: the results are a formula too, whose clauses have one or two literals, and a question that this smaller formula answers with “no” has the answer “no” in the model.

The graphs translate the model into a list of rules about one or two features. Anything that this list forbids, the model forbids: that is why a “no” is always right. Nothing that the model says about one or two features is missing from the list: that is why the graphs are complete for pairs. What the model says about three or more features at once is all that can be missing. Nothing else in the vignettes needs this section.

The results as a formula

Notation. Let φ\varphi be the formula that variplex analyses, a conjunction of clauses (Looking at the formula), and let VV be the features that the results name: those that can vary (the dots of the graphs) and the core and dead ones. The other variables of φ\varphi, the helpers of a translation and the abstract features, are not in VV. A solution σ\sigma of a formula gives each of its variables the value true or false so that the formula holds, σ⊨φ\sigma \vDash \varphi; SAT(ψ)\mathrm{SAT}(\psi) says that ψ\psi has a solution and UNSAT(ψ)\mathrm{UNSAT}(\psi) that it has none. φ\varphi has solutions: otherwise the model is void, and vp_generate() writes no results. A configuration is the restriction σ|V\sigma|_V of a solution of φ\varphi to the features of VV. For a formula ψ\psi over VV, φ⊨ψ\varphi \vDash \psi means that every solution of φ\varphi satisfies ψ\psi, that is, every configuration does. Literals are written ℓ\ell, and ¬ℓ\lnot\ell is the opposite of ℓ\ell.

The results. Each result is a clause over VV:

Result Clause Written when
vv is core vv UNSAT(φ∧¬v)\mathrm{UNSAT}(\varphi \land \lnot v)
vv is dead ¬v\lnot v UNSAT(φ∧v)\mathrm{UNSAT}(\varphi \land v)
arrow a→ba \to b (requires) ¬a∨b\lnot a \lor b UNSAT(φ∧a∧¬b)\mathrm{UNSAT}(\varphi \land a \land \lnot b)
red line aa — bb (excludes) ¬a∨¬b\lnot a \lor \lnot b UNSAT(φ∧a∧b)\mathrm{UNSAT}(\varphi \land a \land b)
green line aa — bb (at least one, or_graph = TRUE) a∨ba \lor b UNSAT(φ∧¬a∧¬b)\mathrm{UNSAT}(\varphi \land \lnot a \land \lnot b)

Let δ\delta be the conjunction of all these clauses. Each has one or two literals: δ\delta is a 2-CNF, and the graphs are a translation of φ\varphi into one. The last column is how variplex finds the clauses (Core, dead and variable features). It computes the backbone of φ\varphi, the literals true in every solution, and for every feature aa that can vary the backbone of φ∧a\varphi \land a (and of φ∧¬a\varphi \land \lnot a for the third graph); a literal ℓ\ell belongs to the backbone of ψ\psi exactly when UNSAT(ψ∧¬ℓ)\mathrm{UNSAT}(\psi \land \lnot\ell). So every clause is one answer of the solver: an UNSAT writes it, a SAT leaves it out. The proofs take the answers of the solver as right.

A fact used throughout. For literals ℓ1,…,ℓk\ell_1, \ldots, \ell_k, UNSAT(φ∧ℓ1∧⋯∧ℓk)⇔φ⊨¬ℓ1∨⋯∨¬ℓk,\mathrm{UNSAT}(\varphi \land \ell_1 \land \cdots \land \ell_k) \iff \varphi \vDash \lnot\ell_1 \lor \cdots \lor \lnot\ell_k , because a solution of φ\varphi falsifies the clause on the right only by making ℓ1,…,ℓk\ell_1, \ldots, \ell_k all true.

Everything the results say is true

Theorem 1. φ⊨δ\varphi \vDash \delta: every configuration satisfies every clause of every result.

Proof. Let γ\gamma be a clause of δ\delta. vp_generate() wrote it because φ\varphi conjoined with the opposites of its literals is unsatisfiable, so φ⊨γ\varphi \vDash \gamma by the fact above; and γ\gamma names only features of VV. □

Since φ⊨δ\varphi \vDash \delta, conjoining δ\delta to φ\varphi changes nothing: φ≡δ∧ν\varphi \equiv \delta \land \nu, where ν\nu is what the results leave out (ν=φ\nu = \varphi will do). Hence SAT(φ)⇒SAT(δ)∧SAT(ν)\mathrm{SAT}(\varphi) \Rightarrow \mathrm{SAT}(\delta) \land \mathrm{SAT}(\nu), and read backwards, UNSAT(δ)⇒UNSAT(φ)\mathrm{UNSAT}(\delta) \Rightarrow \mathrm{UNSAT}(\varphi). The same holds with a question. A wish list, or any choice of features to have and not to have, is a conjunction ω\omega of literals over VV, and UNSAT(δ∧ω)⇒UNSAT(φ∧ω).\mathrm{UNSAT}(\delta \land \omega) \;\Rightarrow\; \mathrm{UNSAT}(\varphi \land \omega) . A question that the results answer with “no” has the answer “no” in the model. More generally, δ⊨ψ\delta \vDash \psi implies φ⊨ψ\varphi \vDash \psi for every formula ψ\psi: every consequence drawn from the results (a chain of arrows, an atomic set, a line of the kernel, a step of an explanation) holds in the model.

About one or two features, nothing is missing

Theorem 2. For every clause γ\gamma over VV with at most two literals, φ⊨γ⇔δ⊨γ.\varphi \vDash \gamma \iff \delta \vDash \gamma . (Without or_graph = TRUE, δ\delta has no green lines, and the theorem holds for the clauses that have a negated literal.)

Proof. (⇐\Leftarrow) By Theorem 1. (⇒\Rightarrow) Let φ⊨γ\varphi \vDash \gamma; a clause that names one feature twice is trivial.

  • γ=v\gamma = v. Then UNSAT(φ∧¬v)\mathrm{UNSAT}(\varphi \land \lnot v): vv is core, and vv is a clause of δ\delta. γ=¬v\gamma = \lnot v likewise, with vv dead.

  • γ=ℓa∨ℓb\gamma = \ell_a \lor \ell_b on features aa and bb, and aa is core or dead, so that δ\delta has a clause u∈{a,¬a}u \in \{a, \lnot a\}. If u=ℓau = \ell_a, then δ⊨γ\delta \vDash \gamma. Otherwise ℓa\ell_a is false in every configuration, so φ⊨ℓb\varphi \vDash \ell_b; by the first case ℓb\ell_b is a clause of δ\delta, and δ⊨γ\delta \vDash \gamma.

  • γ=ℓa∨ℓb\gamma = \ell_a \lor \ell_b and both features can vary. The four possible clauses, ¬a∨b\lnot a \lor b, a∨¬ba \lor \lnot b, ¬a∨¬b\lnot a \lor \lnot b and a∨ba \lor b, are an arrow a→ba \to b, an arrow b→ab \to a, a red line and a green line. variplex asks the solver about each of them, and since φ⊨γ\varphi \vDash \gamma the answer is UNSAT: γ\gamma is a clause of δ\delta. □

This is the second column of What is always true, and what may be missing. Every core and every dead feature is found. Two features that are always selected together, φ⊨(¬a∨b)∧(¬b∨a)\varphi \vDash (\lnot a \lor b) \land (\lnot b \lor a), are joined by arrows both ways: the atomic sets are complete. And every question about one or two features gets the answer of the model, since UNSAT(φ∧ℓ1∧ℓ2)\mathrm{UNSAT}(\varphi \land \ell_1 \land \ell_2) is φ⊨¬ℓ1∨¬ℓ2\varphi \vDash \lnot\ell_1 \lor \lnot\ell_2. Both answers of the solver are at work: UNSAT makes the graphs true (Theorem 1), and SAT, whose solution is a configuration that breaks the missing link, makes them complete for pairs (Theorem 2).

Theorem 3. For every 2-CNF formula ψ\psi over VV, φ⊨ψ\varphi \vDash \psi implies δ⊨ψ\delta \vDash \psi.

Proof. Every clause of ψ\psi has at most two literals and is implied by φ\varphi, hence by δ\delta (Theorem 2). □

So δ\delta is the strongest 2-CNF formula over VV that φ\varphi implies, its least upper bound among the 2-CNF formulas in the terms of knowledge compilation Selman and Kautz (1996): the best description of the model that a formula of pairs can give. What the graphs miss, no graph of pairs could hold.

A wish list is decided by its pairs

Theorem 4. Let ω\omega be a set of literals over VV that holds no feature together with its opposite: features that a product must have and, with the third graph, features that it must not have. Then UNSAT(δ∧ω)\mathrm{UNSAT}(\delta \land \omega) exactly when ω\omega falsifies a clause of δ\delta, that is, when one literal of ω\omega is the opposite of a clause of one literal of δ\delta (a wanted feature is dead, an unwanted one core), or two literals of ω\omega are the opposites of a clause of two literals (two wanted features joined by a red line, a wanted feature with an arrow to an unwanted one, two unwanted features joined by a green line).

Proof. If ω\omega falsifies a clause of δ\delta, δ∧ω\delta \land \omega has no solution. For the converse, suppose that ω\omega falsifies no clause of δ\delta. Make true the literals of ω\omega and the clauses of one literal of δ\delta, and repeat the first step of every solver, unit propagation: whenever a clause of δ\delta has one literal false and the other undecided, make the other true. Each literal xx made true is reached by a chain of clauses of δ\delta from a literal ww of ω\omega or from a clause of one literal, and resolution, which derives ¬w∨x\lnot w \lor x from ¬w∨y\lnot w \lor y and ¬y∨x\lnot y \lor x, gives δ⊨¬w∨x\delta \vDash \lnot w \lor x (or δ⊨x\delta \vDash x). Suppose that a clause ℓ∨ℓ′\ell \lor \ell' of δ\delta ends with all its literals false (a clause of one literal is the case ℓ=ℓ′\ell = \ell'): ¬ℓ\lnot\ell was reached from w1w_1 and ¬ℓ′\lnot\ell' from w2w_2, and two more resolutions with ℓ∨ℓ′\ell \lor \ell' give δ⊨¬w1∨¬w2\delta \vDash \lnot w_1 \lor \lnot w_2 (a single literal, or no literal at all, when a chain started from a clause of one literal). By Theorem 1, φ\varphi implies that clause too, and by the proof of Theorem 2 it, or a literal of it, is a clause of δ\delta that ω\omega falsifies, against the assumption (no literal at all is impossible, since SAT(δ)\mathrm{SAT}(\delta)). So propagation ends without a falsified clause. Every clause of δ\delta then has a true literal or no decided variable; those of the second kind are satisfied by any solution of δ\delta, which exists because SAT(φ)⇒SAT(δ)\mathrm{SAT}(\varphi) \Rightarrow \mathrm{SAT}(\delta), and its values for the undecided variables, with the decided ones, satisfy δ∧ω\delta \land \omega. □

With wanted features only, the third graph is not needed: the clauses ¬w1∨¬w2\lnot w_1 \lor \lnot w_2 that the proof uses have negated literals, and Theorem 2 holds for them without green lines. This is the question of the kernel (The kernel: “can these go together?”) and of the measure of wish lists (Wish lists): both look at the pairs of the list, and need no solver. A 2-CNF formula can always be decided in time proportional to its size Aspvall et al. (1979), while for a general formula no method is known that is fast in every case: that is the bargain of the graphs.

Beyond pairs, a “yes” can be wrong

Theorem 5. There are φ\varphi and ω\omega, a conjunction of three literals, with SAT(δ∧ω)\mathrm{SAT}(\delta \land \omega) and UNSAT(φ∧ω)\mathrm{UNSAT}(\varphi \land \omega).

Proof. The tiny band of A rule that no pair can show. Its three features are optional, and φ⊨¬𝐺𝑃𝑆∨¬𝑁𝐹𝐶∨¬𝐴𝑙𝑤𝑎𝑦𝑠𝑂𝑛𝐷𝑖𝑠𝑝𝑙𝑎𝑦.\varphi \vDash \lnot \mathit{GPS} \lor \lnot \mathit{NFC} \lor \lnot \mathit{AlwaysOnDisplay} . Each feature, and each pair of them, can be chosen in all ways, so no clause of one or two literals is implied: δ=⊤\delta = \top (vp_generate() wrote no clause). With ω=𝐺𝑃𝑆∧𝑁𝐹𝐶∧𝐴𝑙𝑤𝑎𝑦𝑠𝑂𝑛𝐷𝑖𝑠𝑝𝑙𝑎𝑦\omega = \mathit{GPS} \land \mathit{NFC} \land \mathit{AlwaysOnDisplay}, then, SAT(δ∧ω)\mathrm{SAT}(\delta \land \omega) while UNSAT(φ∧ω)\mathrm{UNSAT}(\varphi \land \omega). □

In general, the assignments of VV that satisfy δ\delta and are not configurations are those that violate ν\nu. By Theorem 3, every part of ν\nu that a 2-CNF formula could express is already in δ\delta; what remains are rules whose shortest clauses have three or more literals. How representative are the graphs? measures how often they matter.

What the theorems say about each result

Result True, because Complete?
Core and dead features each is a clause of δ\delta (Theorem 1) Yes: the clauses of one literal (Theorem 2).
The three graphs each link is a clause of δ\delta (Theorem 1) Yes for pairs (Theorem 2); not beyond (Theorem 5).
Atomic sets the arrows both ways are clauses of δ\delta (Theorem 1) Yes: two clauses of two literals (Theorem 2).
Minimal form vp_expand() gives δ\delta back from it It says what δ\delta says, no more.
Kernel: boxes, arrows, red lines they follow from δ\delta (Theorem 1) No: only what δ\delta says about “can these go together?”.
A “no” to a wish list (kernel, graphs) the list falsifies a clause of δ\delta (Theorem 4), so the model forbids it (Theorem 1) No: a list that only a rule beyond pairs forbids gets a “yes” (Theorem 5).
A “yes” to a wish list (kernel, graphs) not always true (Theorem 5) Yes: a list that can be built falsifies no clause of δ\delta (Theorem 1).
Explanations each step is a clause of δ\delta (Theorem 1) No: it names links, not the rules of the model behind them.
Comparisons it compares the δ\delta of two models, each true of its own model (Theorem 1) No: a change of ν\nu alone leaves δ\delta as it was (the battery rule of The kernel: a “no” is final, a “yes” is a good guess).
Whole products every configuration satisfies δ\delta (Theorem 1) No: δ\delta lets pass assignments that violate ν\nu (Theorem 5).

With numbers

For a UVL model μ\mu with numbers or texts, let φ\varphi be the formula that variplex builds from it (Features that are more than yes or no), and Conf(μ)\mathrm{Conf}(\mu) and Conf(φ)\mathrm{Conf}(\varphi) the configurations of each, taken as the features of VV that a product has. The theorems are about φ\varphi. They carry over to μ\mu when Conf(μ)⊆Conf(φ),\mathrm{Conf}(\mu) \subseteq \mathrm{Conf}(\varphi) , that is, when φ\varphi allows every product of μ\mu and maybe more:

  • This holds when variplex only leaves things out. A constraint left out is a conjunct less, which can only add solutions; a feature with a value is kept by its presence, and every constraint on its value is left out.

  • A feature cardinality is not left out but read as one feature, mandatory or optional as its group says. The inclusion holds unless a feature of a mandatory group may have no copy at all (a cardinality that starts at 0): φ\varphi then says more than μ\mu. variplex warns about every feature cardinality, so that you can check.

Under this condition every clause that φ\varphi implies holds in every product of μ\mu, so Theorem 1 holds for μ\mu: every “no” of the results is a “no” of the model, and UNSAT(φ)\mathrm{UNSAT}(\varphi) means that μ\mu has no product. That is the first column of What is always true, and what may be missing, with numbers. Theorem 2 does not carry over: δ\delta has every clause of two literals that φ\varphi implies, but a rule that only the numbers of μ\mu make, even about two features, is not implied by φ\varphi. In the band with a power budget (Even two features), every product of μ\mu satisfies ¬𝐴𝑙𝑤𝑎𝑦𝑠𝑂𝑛𝐷𝑖𝑠𝑝𝑙𝑎𝑦∨¬𝐺𝑃𝑆\lnot \mathit{AlwaysOnDisplay} \lor \lnot \mathit{GPS}, while φ⊭¬𝐴𝑙𝑤𝑎𝑦𝑠𝑂𝑛𝐷𝑖𝑠𝑝𝑙𝑎𝑦∨¬𝐺𝑃𝑆\varphi \nvDash \lnot \mathit{AlwaysOnDisplay} \lor \lnot \mathit{GPS}. That is the second column.
